adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — [P1, confidence 100] `work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` creates an unbounded queue while `submit` always accepts work, so consumption outruns a slow result processor until queued payloads and offset sets exhaust process memory instead of providing the documented backpressure.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `queue.Queue()` created without a maxsize parameter at line 185, making it unbounded. The `submit` method at line 207 calls `work_queue.put(work_item)` which will never block on an unbounded queue. The docstring at lines 161-168 claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' but this is false - there's no maxsize set, so queues never 'fill up' and no backpressure occurs. If the result_processor is slow, items will accumulate indefinitely in memory. This is a real defect where the documented behavior doesn't match the implementation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:203 — [P1, confidence 100] `partitions: Mapping[Partition, int]` is ignored while every strategy generation shares `self.queue_pool`, so a partition rebalance leaves revoked-partition offsets in the tracker and lets a strategy's commit thread commit offsets through the wrong generation's callback.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue: in create_with_partitions (line 203), the partitions parameter is ignored, and self.queue_pool is shared across partition assignments. When create_with_partitions is called during rebalance, a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy is created but uses the same self.queue_pool (created once in __init__ at line 131-135). The OffsetTracker inside queue_pool accumulates offsets from all partitions ever assigned. On rebalance, revoked partitions' offsets remain in the tracker, and the commit_thread continues committing through the new strategy's commit_function callback. This could cause commits for partitions no longer owned by this consumer, which is a correctness bug in partition rebalance handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:338 — [P1, confidence 100] `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` makes strategy-scoped `close()` destroy the factory-owned shared pool, so the next `create_with_partitions` call after a rebalance returns a strategy backed by stopped workers and submitted messages remain queued forever.

adjudication.rationale: The finding is correct. Looking at the diff: 1) In result_consumer.py, the factory creates `self.queue_pool` as a shared instance (line 133-137). 2) In queue_consumer.py, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (line 338), which sets worker.shutdown=True and calls q.shutdown() on all queues. 3) The factory's `create_with_partitions` method creates new strategies that reference the same `self.queue_pool` instance. After a rebalance triggers close() on the old strategy, the shared pool is destroyed, but the factory still holds a reference to the now-dead pool. New strategies created after rebalance would use this shutdown pool with stopped workers. The factory's own shutdown() method also sets queue_pool=None, but the strategy's close() doesn't, creating inconsistent state.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:89 — [P1, confidence 75] `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)` treats Kafka offsets as a gap-free integer sequence, so a legitimate skipped offset leaves every later completed record permanently uncommittable and grows tracker state without bound.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real issue in the `get_committable_offsets` method. Looking at lines 85-95 in queue_consumer.py, the code iterates `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)` and breaks when it encounters an offset not in `all_offsets`. This assumes Kafka offsets are contiguous. If there's a legitimate gap (e.g., offset 101 was never received but 100 and 102 were), the loop will break at 101 even if 102+ are completed. The test `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` in the diff actually demonstrates this behavior - it sends offsets 100, 102, 103 (skipping 101) and expects only offset 100 to be committable. While this is 'working as designed' for that test case, the finding's concern is valid: if offset 101 is legitimately never going to arrive (compacted topic, producer skip, etc.), offsets 102+ will never be committed and the tracker state grows unbounded since `all_offsets` keeps accumulating.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:144 — [P1, confidence 100] `except Exception:` followed by unconditional `complete_offset` makes the worker/result-processor boundary incapable of representing failure, so a failed result is marked complete and its Kafka offset is committed as if processing succeeded.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in queue_consumer.py lines 130-148, the OrderedQueueWorker.run() method has a try/except/finally structure where the `finally` block unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)`. This means even when an exception occurs in `self.result_processor(self.identifier, work_item.result)` (caught by the broad `except Exception:` at line 144), the offset is still marked as complete. The commit loop in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy will then commit this offset to Kafka, effectively treating a failed message as successfully processed. This is a real bug - failed messages should not have their offsets committed as if they succeeded, as this leads to data loss (the failed message will never be reprocessed).

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:31 — [P2 advisory, confidence 100] `message: Message[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload]` retains the raw message even though no consumer reads the field, so every backlog item duplicates payload lifetime; although it preserves hypothetical future debugging context, deleting the field and constructor argument removes redundant memory and two places that future shape changes must update.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims the `message` field in WorkItem is unused and wastes memory. However, looking at the diff, the `message` field is part of the WorkItem dataclass design. While it's true that the current code doesn't appear to read the `message` field after storing it, this is a design choice for a new feature being added. The finding is essentially a style/optimization suggestion rather than a bug or important issue. The field may be intentionally preserved for debugging, logging, or future use cases. This is a minor optimization suggestion that doesn't represent a defect or important architectural concern - it's more of a premature optimization nit.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:136 — [P1, confidence 100] `num_queues=max_workers or 20` accepts the advertised `--max-workers -1` command, constructs a pool with zero queues, and makes every submitted uptime result hit `ZeroDivisionError` before being marked complete and committed without processing.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that `--max-workers -1` is an 'advertised' command option, but looking at the diff, there's no evidence that -1 is a valid or advertised value. The click.Option for max_workers has `type=int` and `default=None`, with no indication that -1 is a supported value. The code `max_workers or 20` would only result in 0 queues if max_workers is explicitly 0, not -1 (since -1 is truthy in Python). If max_workers=-1, the expression evaluates to -1, not 0. The ZeroDivisionError claim about `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` would only occur with num_queues=0, which requires max_workers=0, not -1. The finding misrepresents how the code works.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:149 — [P1/100] `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` runs from `finally` after `result_processor` throws, so the commit loop acknowledges the failed Kafka record and permanently drops its work instead of retrying it.

adjudication.rationale: The finding is accurate. Looking at lines 143-151 in queue_consumer.py, the `finally` block unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` after the try block that calls `self.result_processor(self.identifier, work_item.result)`. When the result_processor throws an exception (caught by the `except Exception` at line 145), the finally block still marks the offset as complete. This means the commit loop in `_commit_loop` (lines 268-285) will eventually commit this offset, permanently acknowledging the failed message to Kafka. The message's work is lost with no retry mechanism. This is a correctness bug - failed processing should not result in offset commitment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:320 — [P1/100] `add_offset(...)` followed by `complete_offset(...)` in the blanket submission-error handler converts grouping and enqueue failures into committable success, so a decoded record whose grouping or queue insertion fails is logged but irretrievably skipped.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lines 305-323 in queue_consumer.py, the submit method has a try/except block. When an exception occurs during decoding, grouping, or queue submission (lines 306-318), the except block (lines 319-323) logs the error and then calls add_offset followed by complete_offset. This marks the offset as successfully processed even though the message was never actually processed. This means if grouping_fn raises an exception or queue_pool.submit fails, the message is silently skipped and the offset is committed, causing data loss. The finding correctly identifies this as a bug where failures in the submission path are converted to committable success.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:338 — [P1/100] `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` closes the factory-owned pool when Arroyo closes a strategy on partition revocation, and the next `create_with_partitions` reuses that closed pool so every reassigned record fails enqueue and is acknowledged without processing.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real bug. Looking at the diff: 1) In ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__, queue_pool is created once and stored as self.queue_pool (line 128-132). 2) In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and terminate() (lines 337-341), self.queue_pool.shutdown() is called. 3) In ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() (lines 182-184), queue_pool.shutdown() is called and queue_pool is set to None. However, the strategy's close()/terminate() methods call queue_pool.shutdown() directly on the pool reference they hold, not through the factory. When Arroyo revokes partitions and calls strategy.close(), the pool gets shutdown. But the factory still holds the same pool reference (until factory.shutdown() is called). If create_with_partitions is called again for reassignment, it reuses the same (now shutdown) queue_pool since thread_queue_parallel is still True but the pool was already shutdown. The FixedQueuePool.shutdown() method (lines 227-236) sets worker.shutdown=True and calls q.shutdown() on all queues, making them unusable for future submissions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:233 — [P1/100] `worker.shutdown = True` is set before the queues are drained, so graceful shutdown exits each worker after at most its current item and returns with queued records unprocessed; broker redelivery prevents outright loss but still causes delayed and duplicate side effects for in-flight work.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the shutdown() method in FixedQueuePool (lines 224-236), the code first sets `worker.shutdown = True` for all workers, then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` on queues, then joins workers. In OrderedQueueWorker.run() (lines 117-145), the worker checks `while not self.shutdown` before trying to get from the queue. If shutdown=True is set while items are still in the queue, the worker will exit the loop after processing at most its current item, leaving queued items unprocessed. The queue.shutdown(immediate=False) is called after setting worker.shutdown=True, so workers may exit before the queue signals them to drain. This is a real ordering bug that could cause items to be left unprocessed during shutdown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:185 — [P2/75] `queue.Queue()` creates an unbounded queue and `submit` never throttles polling, so sustained input above worker throughput grows retained Kafka payloads until the consumer exhausts memory; per-poll broker limits only bound each increment and do not bound the accumulated backlog.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that FixedQueuePool creates unbounded queues (line 185: `queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()`) and the submit method (lines 199-205) adds items without any backpressure mechanism. The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() method (lines 280-310) also has no throttling. While the poll() method reports metrics on queue depth, there's no mechanism to slow down or reject submissions when queues grow large. This means if messages arrive faster than workers can process them, memory will grow unbounded. This is a real correctness/resource exhaustion bug in the new code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:226 — [P2/75] `get_stats()["total_items"] == 0` treats an item removed by a worker as finished while its processor is still running, so callers of `wait_until_empty` proceed during active work and violate the method's completion contract; `Queue.qsize()` being intentionally approximate does not supply an in-flight completion signal.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a race condition in `wait_until_empty`. Looking at the diff, `get_stats()` returns `sum(queue_depths)` where `queue_depths = [q.qsize() for q in self.queues]`. When a worker calls `work_queue.get()`, the item is removed from the queue (reducing qsize), but the worker hasn't finished processing yet - it still needs to call `result_processor` and then `complete_offset`. So `wait_until_empty` can return True while workers are still actively processing items. The method's docstring says 'Wait until all queues are empty' but this doesn't guarantee processing completion. This is a real correctness bug - callers expecting all work to be done when this returns True will be wrong.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:106 — [P2, confidence 100] `assert len(queue_indices) == 3` depends on randomized Python hashes and fails under `PYTHONHASHSEED=211` even though queue assignment works, making the suite flaky.

adjudication.rationale: The test at line 106 asserts `assert len(queue_indices) == 3` expecting that 20 different group keys will be distributed across all 3 queues. The `get_queue_for_group` method uses `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` (line 186-187 in queue_consumer.py). Python's `hash()` function for strings is randomized by default (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the distribution of 20 groups across 3 queues is not guaranteed to cover all 3 queues with every seed. This is a real flaky test bug - the test assumes uniform distribution but hash randomization can cause all 20 groups to map to fewer than 3 queues with certain seeds.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:161 — [P1, confidence 100] `assert self.process_complete_event.wait(timeout=5.0)` plus the count/group assertions only prove eventual processing, so a fully serial implementation passes `test_concurrent_processing_across_groups` and concurrency regressions ship undetected.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that test_concurrent_processing_across_groups in the new test file only verifies that 6 items are eventually processed and that 3 different groups were seen. It uses wait(timeout=5.0) and checks len(self.processed_items) == 6, but doesn't actually verify concurrent execution timing. A serial implementation would pass this test. This is a valid concern about test coverage for the new thread-queue-parallel feature - the test claims to verify concurrent processing but doesn't actually measure concurrency (e.g., via timing or tracking simultaneous execution). This is a real test gap for newly added functionality.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:200 — [P2, confidence 100] `assert stats["total_items"] > 0` races the already-started worker threads, which drain all ten items before this assertion under valid scheduling and produce a spurious test failure.

adjudication.rationale: The test at line 200 submits 10 work items to the queue pool, then immediately checks `assert stats["total_items"] > 0`. However, the worker threads are already running (started in setUp via `worker.start()`), so they can drain all items before the assertion executes. This is a race condition - under valid scheduling where workers are fast, all 10 items could be processed before `get_stats()` is called, causing `total_items` to be 0 and the assertion to fail spuriously. The test later waits for processing to complete, but the intermediate assertion is racy.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:312 — [P1, confidence 100] `assert len(self.processed_results) == 5` never compares result order, so reversed or arbitrarily reordered processing passes `test_preserves_order_within_group` and leaves the feature's core ordering guarantee unverified.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the test `test_preserves_order_within_group` in the diff (lines 296-312), the test creates 5 messages for the same subscription, submits them in order, and then only asserts `assert len(self.processed_results) == 5`. The finding correctly identifies that this test does NOT verify the order of processing - it only checks that 5 items were processed. The test name claims to verify order preservation but the assertion doesn't actually check order. This is a legitimate test gap for a feature whose core guarantee is ordering within groups. The test should compare `processed_results` order against expected order, similar to how `test_ordered_processing_within_group` in TestFixedQueuePool does verify order with `assert group_items == ['item_0', 'item_1', 'item_2', 'item_3', 'item_4']`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:323 — [P1, confidence 100] `assert self.process_complete_event.wait(timeout=5.0)` and `assert len(self.processed_results) == 4` never establish overlap, so a one-worker serial strategy passes `test_concurrent_processing_different_groups` and concurrency regressions remain green.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that test_concurrent_processing_different_groups only verifies that 4 items were processed, not that they were processed concurrently. The test submits 4 messages to different groups and waits for completion, then asserts len(self.processed_results) == 4. This would pass even with serial processing. However, this is a test quality issue (missing assertion for concurrency) rather than a bug in the production code. The test name suggests it should verify concurrent processing but doesn't actually test for parallelism/overlap.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1820 — [P1, confidence 100] `assert mock_processor_call.call_count == 2` proves only that both mocked calls eventually ran, so `test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions` passes when the subscriptions execute serially and fails to protect the advertised parallelism.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions only asserts that mock_processor_call.call_count == 2, which verifies both messages were processed but doesn't actually verify concurrent/parallel execution. The test name claims to test 'concurrent processing' but the assertion would pass even if messages were processed serially. This is a valid test coverage gap - the test doesn't verify the parallelism property it claims to test. However, this is not a bug in the production code, just an incomplete test that doesn't fully validate the advertised behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:1922 — [P1, confidence 100] `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` explicitly accepts zero commits after an error, so the test passes without verifying its stated guarantee that later successful messages remain committable.

adjudication.rationale: The test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` claims to verify 'that errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages' but the assertion `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` actually accepts the case where NO commits happen at all. This means the test doesn't verify its stated purpose - that successful messages after an error can still be committed. The test passes trivially if the system commits nothing, which doesn't validate the error isolation behavior. This is a real test quality issue in newly added test code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py:2005 — [P1, confidence 100] `assert factory.queue_pool is None` checks only reference clearing, so `test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown` passes when shutdown discards queued results instead of draining them.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test `test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown` only verifies that `factory.queue_pool is None` after shutdown, but doesn't verify that queued items were actually processed before shutdown. Looking at the diff, the test submits 5 results and then immediately calls `factory.shutdown()` without waiting for processing to complete. The `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` method (lines 227-237) sets `worker.shutdown = True` and calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`, but the test doesn't verify the items were drained. This is a legitimate test coverage gap - the test name suggests it should verify 'graceful' shutdown (processing remaining items), but it only checks the reference is cleared.
